newsitem.title: GERMANY: ATHLETICS-TIEDTKE TO MAKE CONTROVERSIAL COMEBACK AFTER DOPING.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-TIEDTKE TO MAKE CONTROVERSIAL COMEBACK AFTER DOPING.

text.p: German long jumper Susen Tiedtke will make a controversial return to athletics after a drugs ban next week and fuel criticism that the sport's tough stance on doping is on its last legs.

Tiedtke, a former double world indoor medallist, said on Wednesday that she would compete in a meeting in Johannesburg next Monday just days after a two-year ban for taking steroids came to an end this week.

While German law has made clear that the former East German can return to competition, the sight of her blonde locks on a long jump runway is likely to cause alarm among those who believe that athletics should hand out tough penalties to drug cheats.
The sport's ruling body is now almost certain to be forced to change its rules in the next few months and cut maximum bans for doping from four to two years, ending a campaign which began in 1991.

Tiedtke's case is controversial because, under the rules of the International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) -- the sport's governing body -- she should have served a four-year ban, the compulsory sentence for steroid use.

But the doping cases of former double world sprint champion Katrin Krabbe in 1992, which ended up in the civil courts, have forced German athletics chiefs to reduce bans to two years because anything longer is unacceptable by German law.
Athletics now has a situation where doping offenders are facing different sanctions depending on their nationality.

Tiedtke, who married the former American Olympic long jump bronze medallist Joe Greene and spends a great deal of time in the U.S., tested positive for steroids the day after she won a bronze medal at the world indoor championships in Barcelona in March 1995.
She claimed innocence and said she had never taken drugs.
Now she is confident of making a huge impact in the sport.

"I'm not looking back, only forward," the 28-year-old said. "I want to be the number one and I'm going for it. I know what I can do. I want to get a medal at the world championships (in August) and possibly win gold at the 2000 Olympics."
The IAAF has yet to approve Tiedtke's comeback officially but it is not expected to stand in her way and will rule that she can compete under rules of "extraordinary circumstances".
German distance runner Martin Bremer, who was also banned for four years in October 1994 for steroid use, is also expected to be allowed to return early.

IAAF chiefs will now urge the congress to change its rules when it meets just before the world championships in Athens. Spain and Austria are among several countries said to be experiencing the same legal problems as Germany.
In 1995, at a meeting in Gothenburg, the congress rejected a proposal to reduce the maximum ban.

Tiedtke will avoid a great deal of German media attention by returning in South Africa but the choice of venue is ironic. It was in South Africa that Krabbe was first accused of manipulating doping samples and where the whole legal battle began.
